source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 31% of people in Korea were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%.
39.6% of health spending in Korea was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
35% of hospital care costs in Korea were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
41% of outpatient medical care costs in Korea were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
64% of dental care costs in Korea were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
49% of pharmaceutical costs in Korea were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
In Greece and Korea, financial coverage for the cost of inpatient care from public sources was only around two-thirds of total costs.
Financial coverage for outpatient care was under 60% in Latvia, Israel, Portugal, Italy and Korea.
The share was less than 2% in Poland, Luxembourg, Colombia and Türkiye, but stood above 5% in Switzerland, Korea and Chile (Figure 5.8).
In general, doctors were more evenly distributed across regions in Belgium, Japan and Korea.
In 2023, the average number of annual in-person doctor consultations per person among OECD countries ranged from fewer than 3 in Mexico, Costa Rica, Sweden and Greece to 18 in Korea (Figure 5.16).

Teleconsultations comprised over 25% of all doctor consultations in Denmark, Estonia, Israel, Portugal and Sweden, but remained very low in Chile, Germany, Greece and Korea (see the section on “Data and digital” in Chapter 9 for trends in teleconsultations).
In some countries, doctors are paid predominantly by fee-for-service (as in Germany, Japan, Korea and the Slovak Republic).

In Korea, this can be explained in part by short consultation times, allowing doctors to treat more patients per session, and seen by the government as a way of keeping waiting times low, with most patients able to receive primary medical care on the same day, even without an appointment.
Iceland, Portugal, Italy, Korea and Sweden reported rates lower than 12 per 100 000 population, while Chile, Czechia, Slovenia and Germany reported rates higher than 40 per 100 000.
